document.title: MuonQ: Enhancing Low-Bit Muon Quantization via Directional Fidelity Optimization

creator.personname: Yupeng Su, Ruijie Zhang, Ziyue Liu, Yequan Zhao, Zheng Zhang University of California, Santa Barbara {yupengsu, zzhang01}@ucsb.edu

abstract.name: Abstract
abstract.p: The Muon optimizer has emerged as a compelling alternative to Adam for training large language models, achieving remarkable computational savings through gradient orthogonalization. However, Muon’s optimizer state is more sensitive to quantization errors: because the orthogonalization discards the magnitudes of singular values and retains only directional information, even small quantization errors in singular vector directions are amplified in the update. In this work, we propose MuonQ, a low-bit Muon training framework built on the principle of directional fidelity optimization. First, we apply a pre-quantization normalization so that each step introduces quantization errors of the same magnitude, preventing the accumulated error from developing a preferred direction. Second, we introduce a structural decomposition that separately quantizes the dominant singular components via power iteration, ensuring that quantization errors perturb only singular value magnitudes rather than rotating singular vector directions. Third, we adopt μ𝜇\mu-law companding quantization to allocate higher resolution to densely packed momentum values, shifting the quantization objective from outlier preservation to dense-region distinguishability. Together, these techniques enable stable 4-bit quantization of Muon’s optimizer states. Pre-training experiments on GPT-style and LLaMA-style models demonstrate that MuonQ at 4-bit precision closely matches full-precision Muon in both training loss and downstream task accuracy, while reducing optimizer state memory by up to 7.3 ×\times. Our code is available at https://github.com/YupengSu/MuonQ.

para.p: Large language models (LLMs) have made transformative impacts across a broad spectrum of domains, including natural language understanding, code generation, and mathematical reasoning. However, as model scale increases following established scaling laws (Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022), the memory required for training has become a critical bottleneck. Modern adaptive optimizers such as Adam (Kingma and Ba, 2015) and AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019) maintain first- and second-order moment estimates for every trainable parameter, resulting in a memory overhead of at least twice the size of the model itself. A growing body of work has demonstrated that these states can be aggressively compressed (Dettmers et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025), without significant degradation in training quality.

Meanwhile, the Muon optimizer (Jordan et al., 2024) has emerged as a compelling alternative to Adam for LLM training. By orthogonalizing the gradient momentum via Newton-Schulz iterations, Muon achieves spectrally controlled updates that yield faster convergence and up to 2×2\times computational savings over AdamW, as validated at scales reaching 16 billion parameters (Liu et al., 2025). A growing body of work has also begun to investigate the quantization of Muon’s optimizer states. Gupta et al. (2025) showed that 8-bit blockwise quantization preserves Muon’s performance reliably, and theoretical analysis has further suggested that Muon is inherently more robust to quantization than Adam (Tang et al., 2026). However, pushing to 4-bit remains challenging: naive uniform quantization leads to significant degradation, and current approaches resort to mixed-precision schemes that keep the dominant singular components at higher precision (Wu et al., 2026).

In this work, we propose MuonQ, a low-bit Muon training framework that enables pure 4-bit quantization via directional fidelity optimization. Prior quantization methods for Muon focus primarily on numerical fidelity, minimizing the reconstruction error of the momentum. However, we observe that Muon’s polar decomposition discards singular value magnitudes and retains only directional information, so quantization errors that perturb singular vector directions are fully preserved in the update. The appropriate objective is therefore to preserve the directional structure of the momentum rather than its element-wise accuracy. Guided by this principle, we make the following contributions:

Pre-quantization normalization for uniform error accumulation (§3.1). We normalize gradients and momentum before quantization so that each step introduces quantization errors of the same magnitude, preventing the accumulated error from developing a preferred direction.

Structural decomposition for stable orthogonalization (§3.2). We show that orthogonalization amplifies quantization errors. By decomposing the momentum and quantizing the singular factors independently, we ensure that quantization errors perturb only singular value magnitudes rather than rotating singular vector directions. A truncated top-k𝑘k variant further balances memory and accuracy.

Companding quantization for dense-region distinguishability (§3.3). Muon requires high resolution near zero due to equal weighting of singular directions. We apply μ𝜇\mu-law companding to reallocate quantization bins toward this dense region.

Together, these techniques enable stable pure 4-bit quantization of Muon’s optimizer states. Pre-training experiments on GPT-style and LLaMA-style models demonstrate that MuonQ at 4-bit precision closely matches full-precision Muon in both training loss and downstream task accuracy, while reducing optimizer state memory by up to 7.3 ×\times.

The Muon optimizer (Jordan et al., 2024) is designed for matrix-shaped parameters in neural network hidden layers. Unlike Adam, which maintains per-element first and second moment estimates, Muon applies a matrix-level orthogonalization to the gradient momentum, producing spectrally controlled updates. Specifically, for a matrix-shaped parameter 𝐖∈ℝm×n𝐖superscriptℝ𝑚𝑛\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}, let 𝐆t=∇𝐖ℒtsubscript𝐆𝑡subscript∇𝐖subscriptℒ𝑡\mathbf{G}_{t}=\nabla_{\mathbf{W}}\mathcal{L}_{t} denote the gradient at step t𝑡t. Muon maintains a momentum buffer 𝐌tsubscript𝐌𝑡\mathbf{M}_{t} and computes updates through the following procedure:

Math.text: formulae@(M _ t = beta * M _ (t - 1) + G _ t, W _ t = W _ (t - 1) - eta * polar * M _ t)

para.p: where β𝛽\beta is the momentum coefficient, η𝜂\eta is the learning rate, and polar⁢(⋅)polar⋅\mathrm{polar}(\cdot) denotes the orthogonal polar factor of a matrix. For a matrix with singular value decomposition 𝐌t=𝐔⁢𝚺⁢𝐕⊤subscript𝐌𝑡𝐔𝚺superscript𝐕top\mathbf{M}_{t}=\mathbf{U}\mathbf{\Sigma}\mathbf{V}^{\top}, this is defined as polar⁢(𝐌t)=𝐔𝐕⊤polarsubscript𝐌𝑡superscript𝐔𝐕top\mathrm{polar}(\mathbf{M}_{t})=\mathbf{U}\mathbf{V}^{\top}. The polar factor replaces all singular values of the momentum with ones, yielding a spectrally flat update that prevents any single direction from dominating the optimization trajectory (Bernstein and Newhouse, 2024). In practice, polar⁢(⋅)polar⋅\mathrm{polar}(\cdot) is efficiently approximated via Newton–Schulz iterations or improved variants such as Polar Express (Amsel et al., 2026).

Given an input tensor 𝐱𝐱\mathbf{x}, the standard b𝑏b-bit symmetric uniform quantization at granularity g𝑔g partitions 𝐱𝐱\mathbf{x} into groups and computes a per-group scale factor and integer codes as:

Math.text: formulae@(s = maximum@(absolute-value@(x)) / (2 ^ (b - 1) - 1), q = clamp * vector@(round * (x / s), (- 2 ^ (b - 1)) + 1, 2 ^ (b - 1) - 1))

para.p: where 𝐬𝐬\mathbf{s} is the scale factor computed over each granularity group and 𝐪∈ℤ|𝐱|𝐪superscriptℤ𝐱\mathbf{q}\in\mathbb{Z}^{|\mathbf{x}|} is the corresponding integer code. The dequantization operator reconstructs the approximation:

Math.text: hat@(x) = Dequant * open-interval@(q, s) = q cdot s

para.p: In this section, we present MuonQ, a unified framework for stable pure 4-bit quantization of Muon’s optimizer states, grounded in the principle of directional fidelity optimization. As discussed in Section 2, Muon’s polar decomposition discards singular value magnitudes and retains only directional information, making the optimizer state uniquely sensitive to directional perturbations introduced by quantization. MuonQ addresses this sensitivity through three complementary techniques: pre-quantization normalization to prevent non-uniform error accumulation (§3.1), structural decomposition to ensure momentum orthogonalization stability (§3.2), and μ𝜇\mu-law companding quantization to improve resolution in the dense near-zero region (§3.3). Algorithm 1 summarizes the complete procedure, and the subsequent subsections detail each component in order.

For evaluating quantization quality, beyond the standard relative error (RE) that measures numerical fidelity, we additionally adopt the cosine similarity (CS) to directly assess directional fidelity, which is what Muon’s polar decomposition ultimately relies on. Formally, for two matrices 𝐀𝐀\mathbf{A}, 𝐁𝐁\mathbf{B} and Frobenius inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩Fsubscript⋅⋅𝐹\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{F}, we define:

Math.text: formulae@(RE * open-interval@(A, B) = (norm@(A - B)) _ F / (norm@(A)) _ F, CS * open-interval@(A, B) = (list@(A, B)) _ F / ((norm@(A)) _ F cdot (norm@(B)) _ F))

para.p: The first step of MuonQ addresses the long-term stability of quantized training by examining how quantization errors accumulate across the momentum update 𝐌t=β⁢𝐌t−1+𝐆tsubscript𝐌𝑡𝛽subscript𝐌𝑡1subscript𝐆𝑡\mathbf{M}_{t}=\beta\mathbf{M}_{t-1}+\mathbf{G}_{t}.

In practice, the norms of 𝐆tsubscript𝐆𝑡\mathbf{G}_{t} and 𝐌tsubscript𝐌𝑡\mathbf{M}_{t} vary substantially across steps, causing the quantization error magnitude to fluctuate from step to step. When accumulated through the momentum recursion, these non-uniformly scaled errors develop a preferred direction, producing anisotropic drift. Since Muon’s polar decomposition is sensitive to directional perturbations, such drift directly degrades update quality over time. As shown by the red curves in Figure 1, without normalization, both the relative error and cosine similarity decline consistently as training progresses.

figure.toccaption: 1Quantization error accumulation over 50 momentum update steps.

caption.text: Quantization error accumulation over 50 momentum update steps.

para.p: We observe that if every quantization step introduces errors of the same magnitude, then the accumulated error behaves as a sum of identically scaled random perturbations, which remains approximately isotropic and does not develop a preferred direction. To achieve this, we normalize both the gradient and momentum to unit Frobenius norm before quantization at each step:

Math.text: formulae@(M _ t = beta * (hat@(M)) _ (t - 1) + G _ t / (norm@(G _ t)) _ F, (bar@(M)) _ t = M _ t / (norm@(M _ t)) _ F)

para.p: The normalized 𝐌¯tsubscript¯𝐌𝑡\bar{\mathbf{M}}_{t} is then decomposed and quantized; upon dequantization at the next step, the reconstructed 𝐌^t−1subscript^𝐌𝑡1\hat{\mathbf{M}}_{t-1} is used directly without rescaling. We verify experimentally in ablation study section (§ 4.2) that applying this normalization to full-precision Muon produces training curves indistinguishable from the unnormalized baseline, confirming that the modified recursion does not alter optimization dynamics.
After normalization, the momentum is ready for quantization. However, directly quantizing and then orthogonalizing it leads to severe error amplification. We now address this issue.

The orthogonalization step amplifies the errors of the quantized momentum 𝐌^tsubscript^𝐌𝑡\hat{\mathbf{M}}_{t} substantially (Wu et al., 2026), as shown in Figure 3(a, b). This amplification has a clear spectral explanation. For 𝐌t=𝐔⁢𝚺⁢𝐕⊤subscript𝐌𝑡𝐔𝚺superscript𝐕top\mathbf{M}_{t}=\mathbf{U}\mathbf{\Sigma}\mathbf{V}^{\top}, quantization perturbs both the singular values and the singular vectors. The polar decomposition maps all singular values to unity, which has two consequences: perturbations to singular value magnitudes are absorbed and vanish, but perturbations that rotate singular vector directions are fully retained and amplified, as they are no longer diluted by magnitude variation.

Our key insight is that if quantization errors only perturb the singular values without rotating the singular vectors, then the polar decomposition will naturally eliminate these errors. To achieve this, we decompose the momentum via SVD and quantize each factor independently:

Math.text: formulae@(M _ t = U cdot S, S = Sigma * V ^ top)

para.p: where 𝐔∈ℝm×r𝐔superscriptℝ𝑚𝑟\mathbf{U}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r} contains the left singular vectors and 𝐒∈ℝr×n𝐒superscriptℝ𝑟𝑛\mathbf{S}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times n} encodes the singular values and right singular vectors, with r=min⁡(m,n)𝑟𝑚𝑛r=\min(m,n). The two singular factors are then quantized and dequantized separately:

Math.text: (hat@(M)) _ t = ((Dequant * (Quant ^ col) _ b * U) cdot Dequant) * (Quant ^ row) _ b * S

figure.toccaption: 2Effect of truncation rank k𝑘k on post-orthogonalization error under 4-bit companding quantization.

caption.text: Effect of truncation rank k𝑘k on post-orthogonalization error under 4-bit companding quantization.

para.p: Crucially, the quantization granularity is aligned with the singular structure: 𝐔𝐔\mathbf{U} is quantized column-wise so that each left singular vector 𝐮isubscript𝐮𝑖\mathbf{u}_{i} is quantized independently, and 𝐒𝐒\mathbf{S} is quantized row-wise so that each scaled right singular vector σi⁢𝐯i⊤subscript𝜎𝑖superscriptsubscript𝐯𝑖top\sigma_{i}\mathbf{v}_{i}^{\top} forms its own quantization group. Since the quantization scale factor is computed independently within each group, errors are confined to scaling each singular component individually without mixing or rotating different singular directions. Figure 3(c, d) confirms this: although decomposition slightly increases pre-orthogonalization error, it eliminates the error amplification caused by orthogonalization.

Without decomposition (a, b), orthogonalization amplifies quantization error severely. With decomposition (c, d), directional fidelity is preserved through orthogonalization.

Without decomposition (a, b), orthogonalization amplifies quantization error severely. With decomposition (c, d), directional fidelity is preserved through orthogonalization.

paragraph.title: Truncation rank as a practical trade-off.

para.p: In practice, polar approximation methods such as Newton–Schulz do not effectively amplify directions associated with very small singular values. Instead, error amplification is dominated by the principal singular subspace. Since quantization errors are primarily induced along the dominant singular directions of the original momentum (Wu et al., 2026), it suffices to align the quantization error with this subspace, without explicitly preserving the full spectrum. Concretely, we decompose:

Math.text: formulae@(M _ t approximately-equals U _ k * S _ k + R _ k, S _ k = Sigma _ k * (V _ k) ^ top)

para.p: where 𝐔k∈ℝm×ksubscript𝐔𝑘superscriptℝ𝑚𝑘\mathbf{U}_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times k} and 𝐒k∈ℝk×nsubscript𝐒𝑘superscriptℝ𝑘𝑛\mathbf{S}_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times n} capture the top-k𝑘k singular components, and 𝐑ksubscript𝐑𝑘\mathbf{R}_{k} is the residual. Because the additional storage scales with k𝑘k rather than min⁡(m,n)𝑚𝑛\min(m,n), the memory overhead remains modest. Following prior work (Ahn et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026), we adopt power iteration to extract the top-k𝑘k components efficiently. Given 𝐒t−1∈ℝk×nsubscript𝐒𝑡1superscriptℝ𝑘𝑛\mathbf{S}_{t-1}\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times n} warm-started from the previous step, we iterate and recover the decomposition as:

Math.text: formulae@(V _ (t - 1) = RowNorm * S _ (t - 1), formulae@(U _ t = orth * M _ t * (V _ (t - 1)) ^ top, S _ t = (U _ t) ^ top * M _ t))

para.p: Figure 2 shows the effect of the truncation rank on post-orthogonalization error. Both RE and CS improve rapidly with increasing k𝑘k and plateau around k/min⁡(m,n)=1/4𝑘𝑚𝑛14k/\min(m,n)=1/4, indicating that a modest rank fraction is sufficient to capture the dominant directional error.

The final component of MuonQ optimizes the quantization operation itself. After normalization and decomposition, each component needs to be quantized to low precision. We now address how to design the quantizer for Muon’s specific value distribution.

paragraph.title: From outlier preservation to dense-region distinguishability.

figure.toccaption: 4Normalized Muon momentum distribution (top) and quantization interval comparison (bottom). Each colored block represents one quantization bin.

caption.text: Normalized Muon momentum distribution (top) and quantization interval comparison (bottom). Each colored block represents one quantization bin.

para.p: As illustrated in Figure 4, the value distribution of 𝐌tsubscript𝐌𝑡\mathbf{M}_{t} exhibits a sharp peak near zero with heavy tails. Under uniform quantization, equal-width bins waste resolution on sparsely populated tails while providing insufficient precision for the dense center. For Adam, its element-wise update is dominated by large-magnitude states, so prior quantization methods (Dettmers et al., 2022) need only preserve outliers and can safely ignore the dense region. However, Muon’s polar decomposition equalizes all singular directions, meaning the dense, small-magnitude entries carry equal directional importance. The critical requirement thus shifts from outlier preservation to distinguishability among closely packed values near zero.

We address this resolution imbalance by applying companding quantization, a classical technique from signal processing (Smith, 1957) that reshapes the value distribution prior to quantization. Companding wraps the base quantizer with a nonlinear transform: a compressing function f𝑓f is applied before quantization, and its inverse f−1superscript𝑓1f^{-1} after dequantization. We adopt the μ𝜇\mu-law function (ITU-T, 1988):

Math.text: formulae@(f * x = sgn * x * (natural-logarithm@(1 + mu * absolute-value@(x)) / natural-logarithm@(1 + mu)), - 1 <= x <= 1)

para.p: where we set μ=255𝜇255\mu=255 following the standard μ𝜇\mu-law convention in digital telephony (ITU-T, 1988). The companded quantization and dequantization operators are defined as:

Math.text: formulae@(list@(q, s) = (CQuant _ b) ^ g * x = (Quant _ b) ^ g * f * x, hat@(x) = CDequant * open-interval@(q, s) = f ^ (- 1) * Dequant * open-interval@(q, s))

table.caption: Table 1Effect of μ𝜇\mu-law companding on 4-bit quantization of layers.0.self_attn.k_proj.

para.p: As illustrated in Figure 4, the logarithmic nonlinearity of f𝑓f reshapes how quantization bins are allocated: the uniform band divides the input range into equal-width bins, whereas the companding band concentrates narrower bins near zero while assigning wider bins to the sparsely populated tails. As shown in Table 1, this density-aware reallocation consistently improves reconstruction quality across all granularities.

figure.toccaption: 5Training loss curves for GPT-2 and LLaMA models on FineWeb.

caption.text: Training loss curves for GPT-2 and LLaMA models on FineWeb.

para.p: We evaluate MuonQ on two model families: GPT-2 (Medium, Large) and LLaMA (350M, 1.1B), all trained on FineWeb (Penedo et al., 2024) following the standard Muon protocol (Liu et al., 2025). We compare against three baselines: full-precision Muon (Muon32), and uniform quantization at 8-bit (Muon8) and 4-bit (Muon4). All methods share identical training hyperparameters and differ only in momentum representation. Unless otherwise noted, we apply tensor-wise quantization to the full momentum matrix 𝐌tsubscript𝐌𝑡\mathbf{M}_{t} (Muon8/Muon4) or the residual 𝐑tsubscript𝐑𝑡\mathbf{R}_{t} (MuonQ4) and a truncation rank of k=1/16𝑘116k=1/16. Detailed configurations are provided in Appendix A. All experiments are conducted on NVIDIA A100 GPUs.

Figure 5 shows the training loss curves across four model configurations throughout training. Across all scales, MuonQ4 closely tracks the full-precision Muon32 baseline, demonstrating stable convergence from the early stages of training through to the end. In contrast, naive Muon4 exhibits a persistent loss gap that does not diminish over the course of training. Notably, the advantage of MuonQ4 over naive quantization becomes more pronounced as model scale increases, suggesting that preserving directional fidelity plays an increasingly critical role at larger scales.

Table 2 reports zero-shot accuracy on ARC-Challenge, ARC-Easy (Clark et al., 2018), OpenBookQA (Mihaylov et al., 2018), BoolQ (Clark et al., 2019), HellaSwag (Zellers et al., 2019), PIQA (Bisk et al., 2020), and WinoGrande (Sakaguchi et al., 2021) across all model scales and architectures, evaluated using the lm-evaluation-harness library (Gao et al., 2023). MuonQ4 consistently matches the Muon32 baseline on various benchmarks, demonstrating that our quantization preserves downstream task performance.

para.p: Figure 6 compares validation perplexity and optimizer-state memory across model scales. MuonQ4 closely tracks the Muon32 baseline in PPL across all scales, while reducing optimizer memory by 7.3×7.3\times on average. Compared to Muon4, MuonQ4 incurs only a modest memory increase but recovers the majority of the full-precision performance.
In this section, we ablate the design choices of MuonQ on GPT-2 Small (124M) trained with 1B FineWeb tokens. The best configuration identified here is used for main results in §4.1.

para.p: Table 3 isolates the effect of each technique. Normalization and companding each improve PPL independently with negligible memory overhead, and their combination yields further gains. Structural decomposition introduces a modest memory increase due to the decomposed factors but provides the largest PPL improvement by protecting singular directions through orthogonalization. The full MuonQ achieves the best trade-off between PPL and memory.

para.p: Figure 7 shows the trade-off between validation PPL and optimizer memory as the truncation rank k𝑘k varies. Increasing k𝑘k monotonically improves PPL by preserving more singular directions, but the memory overhead grows due to the additional storage of Utsubscript𝑈𝑡U_{t} and Stsubscript𝑆𝑡S_{t}. PPL improves sharply from k=0𝑘0k=0 (no decomposition) to k=min⁡(m,n)/16𝑘𝑚𝑛16k=\min(m,n)/16, after which the gains diminish while memory continues to rise. We select k=min⁡(m,n)/16𝑘𝑚𝑛16k=\min(m,n)/16 as the default, as it achieves most of the PPL improvement with only a 9.4% memory increase over the baseline.

para.p: Our pre-quantization normalization (§3.1) modifies the momentum recursion by rescaling both the gradient and the momentum at each step. While this changes the relative magnitudes of successive momentum updates, it does not affect the parameter update direction. Figure 8 shows the training loss at three stages of training. The two curves are virtually indistinguishable throughout, with a mean absolute difference of only 0.003 in training loss, confirming that the normalization introduces no measurable perturbation to the optimization dynamics under full precision.

Table 4 compares quantization granularities across methods. MuonQ4 consistently outperforms the Muon4 baseline at every granularity level. Notably, even MuonQ4 with the coarsest tensor-wise granularity (PPL 40.9) surpasses the best Muon4 configuration with row-wise quantization (PPL 42.9), demonstrating that our techniques provide improvements orthogonal to the choice of granularity.

The memory overhead of optimizer states has motivated a rich line of research on efficient alternatives. One family of approaches exploits low-rank or factored structure to reduce state size. Adafactor (Shazeer and Stern, 2018) and CAME (Luo et al., 2023) approximate Adam’s second moment via factored representations, while GaLore (Zhao et al., 2024) and Flora (Hao et al., 2024) project gradients into low-rank subspaces before applying the optimizer. Sign-based methods such as SignSGD (Bernstein et al., 2018) and 1-bit Adam (Tang et al., 2021) compress gradients or momentum to their signs, reducing both memory and communication costs. Other approaches simplify the optimizer state itself: SM3 (Anil et al., 2019) maintains memory proportional to the sum rather than the product of parameter dimensions, and LAMB (You et al., 2020) replaces per-element states with layerwise adaptive rates. LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) takes a different approach by freezing pretrained weights and tuning only low-rank adapters.

A parallel line of work compresses optimizer states via low-precision representation. For Adam and its variants, Dettmers et al. (2022) proposed block-wise dynamic quantization that enables stable 8-bit optimizer states, and subsequent work has pushed compression to 4-bit for both first-order moments (Li et al., 2023) and second-order preconditioners (Wang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025). For the Muon optimizer, Gupta et al. (2025) showed that 8-bit blockwise quantization preserves performance under both linear and dynamic schemes. Wu et al. (2026) identified that orthogonalization amplifies quantization error primarily in the top singular subspace, and proposed preserving these components at 8-bit while compressing the residual to 4-bit with grid quantization. Theoretical analysis has further suggested that Muon is inherently more robust to quantization than Adam (Tang et al., 2026).

We have presented MuonQ, a framework for low-bit quantization of Muon’s optimizer states guided by the principle of directional fidelity. Three complementary techniques address quantization errors at different stages of the Muon pipeline: pre-quantization normalization stabilizes per-step error magnitudes to prevent directional drift accumulation; structural decomposition via power iteration ensure quantization errors perturb only singular value without rotating singular vectors; and μ𝜇\mu-law companding reallocates quantization bins toward the dense center of the momentum distribution where distinguishability matters most. Together, these enable stable 4-bit quantization with up to 7.3×\times optimizer memory reduction. Experiments across GPT-2 and LLaMA models demonstrate that MuonQ closely matches full-precision Muon in both training loss and downstream task accuracy.

Our experiments are conducted at moderate model scales (up to 1.1B parameters), and the structural decomposition introduces per-step overhead from power iteration. Scaling MuonQ to frontier-scale training with distributed parallelism, combining it with gradient compression techniques such as GaLore (Zhao et al., 2024) and low-rank adaptation (Hu et al., 2022), and extending to sub-4-bit or mixed-format (FP8/FP4) regimes are promising directions for future work.

para.p: All experiments use the Muon optimizer for matrix-shaped hidden-layer parameters and AdamW for embeddings and the language modeling head, following the standard Muon training protocol (Liu et al., 2025). Table 7 summarizes the optimizer hyperparameters.

para.p: AdamW uses a learning rate of 0.001 and weight decay of 0.1 for the embedding and LM head parameters across all experiments. NS5 denotes 5-step Newton–Schulz iteration with the standard coefficients (a,b,c)=(3.4445,−4.7750,2.0315)𝑎𝑏𝑐3.44454.77502.0315(a,b,c)=(3.4445,-4.7750,2.0315) (Jordan et al., 2024).

4bit-Muon-GRASP (Wu et al., 2026) shares with MuonQ the observation that orthogonalization amplifies quantization error primarily in the top singular subspace. To address this, GRASP stores the top-k𝑘k singular components at 8-bit precision while compressing the residual to 4-bit, constituting a mixed-precision scheme. However, GRASP does not analyze why decomposing the momentum is itself beneficial independent of the bit-width assigned to the factors. As we showed in §3.2, the key mechanism is aligning quantization granularity with the singular structure: column-wise quantization of 𝐔𝐔\mathbf{U} and row-wise quantization of 𝐒𝐒\mathbf{S} confine errors to singular value perturbations rather than singular vector rotations, making them invisible to the polar projection regardless of whether the factors are stored at 4-bit or 8-bit. We argue that the structural decomposition itself, rather than higher bit-width, is the dominant source of improvement.

We verify this on GPT-2 Small (124M) trained with 1B FineWeb tokens. For each truncation rank k𝑘k, we compare pure 4-bit against mixed-precision (8/4-bit: 8-bit top, 4-bit residual) under two settings: D only (decomposition only) and Full (all MuonQ techniques). Since GRASP adopts grid quantization as its granularity scheme, which differs from MuonQ’s singular-structure-aligned granularity, we use MuonQ’s column-wise/row-wise aligned quantization for both 4-bit and 8/4-bit variants throughout this comparison to isolate the effect of bit-width from the choice of granularity. As shown in Table 8, structural decomposition accounts for the vast majority of the PPL gain over Muon4 (ΔtotalsubscriptΔtotal\Delta_{\text{total}}), while upgrading the top factors to 8-bit yields only marginal additional improvement (ΔmixedsubscriptΔmixed\Delta_{\text{mixed}}). Under the Full setting at rank 1/161161/16, the total improvement is 29.07 while the mixed-precision contribution is only 0.61—just 2% of the total. Moreover, Full 4-bit at rank 1/161161/16 (PPL 40.93, 44.3 MB) outperforms D-only 8/4-bit at the same rank (PPL 41.60, 48.1 MB) in both PPL and memory, showing that optimizing the 4-bit quantizer via companding is more effective than allocating extra bits. At rank 1/4141/4, the 8/4-bit variant already costs 70.9 MB—87.6% of Muon8 (81.0 MB)—largely negating the purpose of low-bit quantization. These results confirm that structural decomposition with granularity alignment is the key mechanism, and that mixed-precision bit assignment is neither necessary nor cost-effective.

para.p: As discussed in §3.2, MuonQ’s structural decomposition requires aligning quantization granularity with the singular structure: column-wise for 𝐔𝐔\mathbf{U} and row-wise for 𝐒𝐒\mathbf{S}. Here we empirically verify that this alignment is critical and that the quantization direction of 𝐒𝐒\mathbf{S} is the dominant factor.

Figure 9 shows the post-orthogonalization singular value spectra under four granularity combinations. The key factor is the quantization direction of 𝐒𝐒\mathbf{S}: row-wise quantization of 𝐒𝐒\mathbf{S} (panels c, d) achieves RE ≈0.19absent0.19\approx 0.19 and CS ≈0.98absent0.98\approx 0.98, while column-wise quantization of 𝐒𝐒\mathbf{S} (panels a, b) degrades to RE ≈0.91absent0.91\approx 0.91 and CS ≈0.47absent0.47\approx 0.47. In contrast, the granularity of 𝐔𝐔\mathbf{U} has negligible effect (comparing a vs. b, or c vs. d), because 𝐔𝐔\mathbf{U} satisfies 𝐔⊤⁢𝐔=𝐈superscript𝐔top𝐔𝐈\mathbf{U}^{\top}\mathbf{U}=\mathbf{I} and its columns are already unit-norm and orthogonal, making them inherently robust to the choice of quantization grouping. This confirms that row-wise quantization of 𝐒𝐒\mathbf{S} is the critical design choice.

para.p: We further validate this with end-to-end training on GPT-2 Small (124M, 1B FineWeb tokens). As shown in Figure 10, the aligned configuration (col-wise 𝐔𝐔\mathbf{U}, row-wise 𝐒𝐒\mathbf{S}) achieves PPL 40.93, outperforming the across configuration (row-wise 𝐔𝐔\mathbf{U}, col-wise 𝐒𝐒\mathbf{S}) at PPL 41.30. Notably, the aligned variant is also more memory-efficient: each quantization group in the aligned scheme requires only k𝑘k scale factors (one per singular direction), whereas the across scheme requires m𝑚m or n𝑛n scale factors (one per matrix row/column), which is significantly larger since k≪min⁡(m,n)much-less-than𝑘𝑚𝑛k\ll\min(m,n). Thus, singular-structure alignment improves both accuracy and memory efficiency simultaneously.

figure.toccaption: 11Effect of companding parameter μ𝜇\mu on 4-bit row-wise quantization.

caption.text: Effect of companding parameter μ𝜇\mu on 4-bit row-wise quantization.

para.p: The μ𝜇\mu-law companding function (Eq. 10) contains a single hyperparameter μ𝜇\mu that controls the degree of nonlinear compression. Following the convention in signal processing, we search over values of the form 2n−1superscript2𝑛12^{n}-1 (i.e., 15, 63, 127, 255, 511, 1023), which correspond to the maximum representable integer under n𝑛n-bit encoding and are the standard choices in ITU-T companding specifications (ITU-T, 1988). Figure 11 shows the effect of μ𝜇\mu on 4-bit row-wise quantization quality, measured on layers.0.self_attn.k_proj. Both RE and CS improve as μ𝜇\mu increases from 15 to 255, as the companding function progressively allocates more bins to the dense near-zero region. Beyond μ=255𝜇255\mu=255, excessive compression distorts the tail values, degrading both metrics. We select μ=255𝜇255\mu=255 (=28−1absentsuperscript281=2^{8}-1) as the default, which corresponds to the standard ITU-T G.711 μ𝜇\mu-law specification and achieves optimal quantization fidelity under row-wise granularity.

figure.toccaption: 12Training loss of MuonQ with deterministic vs. stochastic rounding on GPT-2 Small. Stochastic rounding degrades performance (42.99 vs. 40.93) and increases training variance.

caption.text: Training loss of MuonQ with deterministic vs. stochastic rounding on GPT-2 Small. Stochastic rounding degrades performance (42.99 vs. 40.93) and increases training variance.

para.p: Stochastic rounding is a widely used technique in low-precision training (Gupta et al., 2015) that replaces the deterministic round⁢(⋅)round⋅\mathrm{round}(\cdot) operator with a randomized variant: for a value z𝑧z, it rounds down to ⌊z⌋𝑧\lfloor z\rfloor with probability ⌈z⌉−z𝑧𝑧\lceil z\rceil-z and up to ⌈z⌉𝑧\lceil z\rceil with probability z−⌊z⌋𝑧𝑧z-\lfloor z\rfloor. Unlike deterministic rounding, stochastic rounding is unbiased in expectation, which has been shown to prevent systematic error accumulation in gradient-based optimization. Given that MuonQ’s pre-quantization normalization (§3.1) is also designed to control error accumulation, a natural question is whether stochastic rounding provides complementary benefits.

We evaluate stochastic rounding on GPT-2 Small (124M) with MuonQ at 4-bit, rank k=min⁡(m,n)/16𝑘𝑚𝑛16k=\min(m,n)/16. As shown in Figure 12, stochastic rounding leads to worse training loss than deterministic rounding (final PPL 42.99 vs. 40.93), with noticeably higher variance throughout training. We attribute this to the interaction between stochastic noise and Muon’s polar decomposition: since the polar projection discards magnitude information and preserves only directions, the random perturbations introduced by stochastic rounding do not cancel out over time as they would in element-wise optimizers like Adam, but instead inject persistent directional noise into the update. MuonQ’s deterministic rounding combined with pre-quantization normalization provides a more controlled approach that ensures uniform error magnitude without introducing additional stochasticity.

A recurring theme across recent Muon variants is the critical role of normalization applied at different stages of the update pipeline. The standard implementation normalizes the momentum by its Frobenius norm before the Newton–Schulz iteration to ensure convergence of the polar approximation (Jordan et al., 2024). Beyond this, NorMuon (Li et al., 2025) introduces neuron-wise normalization after orthogonalization to balance per-neuron update magnitudes, while Turbo-Muon (Boissin et al., 2025) applies a spectral preconditioning step before orthogonalization to accelerate Newton–Schulz convergence. More recently, Muon+ (Zhang et al., 2026) demonstrates that a single additional column-row normalization step after the polar factor already yields consistent improvements across model scales. Notably, these methods all improve either efficiency or effectiveness by inserting normalization at different positions, suggesting that Muon is inherently robust to the numerical scale of its input, and that the orthogonal direction, rather than precise magnitude control, is the primary driver of its optimization.
